tasks.description:
**Question.** A large change in a scene is obvious when it happens in plain view. Is it still easy to see when a brief blank hides the moment of change? Rensink, O'Regan and Clark argued that seeing a change needs attention on the object that changes.

**What the observer sees.** Grey with an empty white rectangle for [[param:cue_field]] (in the Experiment 3 sets it holds a cue word), plain grey for [[param:gray_field]], then the flicker: scene A, grey blank, A, blank, changed scene A′, blank, A′, blank, repeating (images [[param:flicker.image]], blanks [[param:flicker.blank]]) for up to [[param:max_flicker]]. The scenes here are generated photo-like images and simple procedural drawings made for this project; they are illustrative stand-ins, not the paper's photographs of real places.

**What they do.** Press [[param:detect_key]] as soon as they see what is changing. Then, on image A with numbered boxes, press the box around the change and an arrow key for its kind (appearing, colour or position). In the paper they described the change aloud.

**What varies.** Whether the changed object is of central or marginal interest (judged from independent short descriptions of each scene) and the kind of change. Other parameter sets remove the blanks, show each image longer (Experiment 2) or add valid or invalid cue words (Experiment 3).

**What is measured.** Time to see the change, counted in alternations (one switch between A and A′ every 640 ms), averaged over trials where both the box and the kind were right. It is a speed measure; identification errors are a check.

**What a result would mean.** Many more alternations for marginal than for central changes with blanks, but quick detection without them, would mean the change is visible yet unseen until attended. The paper reported this. This adaptation's scenes and interest ratings have not been tested with observers, so no result is claimed.
notes: Paper (p. 369, Fig. 1): 27° × 18° images, 3 s cue field, 1 s grey field, 240 ms images, 80 ms blanks, each image twice before switching, up to 60 s; alternations averaged over correct reports only.

Deviation: 12 generated photo-like scene pairs plus 36 procedural pairs replace the paper's 48 photographs; interest was rated by five model descriptions (photos) or a placement rule (procedural) instead of five naive observers.
Deviation: a keyed location (4 boxes) and kind report replaces the spoken description; box count, sizes, keys and 20 s report limits are ASSUMED.
ASSUMED: grey level, cue rectangle size, 500 ms between trials, 640 ms images in the no-blank set.
Missed or unreported scenes are not served again: each scene is seen once.

tasks.description:
**This set.** Experiment 1's control. The blanks are removed, so the change happens in plain view as a visible flicker of the changed part. This checks that the changes are easy to see when nothing hides them.

**Question.** A large change in a scene is obvious when it happens in plain view. Is it still easy to see when the moment of change is hidden, and does knowing where to look help?

**What the observer sees.** Grey with an empty white rectangle for [[param:cue_field]], plain grey for [[param:gray_field]], then scene A and the changed scene A′ replacing each other directly, each held [[param:flicker.image]] with no blank between them, for up to [[param:max_flicker]]. The scenes are generated photo-like images and procedural drawings made for this project, not the paper's photographs.

**What they do.** Press [[param:detect_key]] as soon as they see what is changing, then press the numbered box around the change on image A and an arrow key for its kind (appearing, colour or position).

**What varies.** Whether the changed object is of central or marginal interest and the kind of change; here the blanks are removed.

**What is measured.** Alternations until the change is seen (one switch between A and A′ every 640 ms), on trials where the box and the kind were both right: a speed measure.

**What it can and cannot show.** Quick detection here but slow detection with blanks would show that the blank, not the change's size or visibility, causes the difficulty; the paper reported 1.4 alternations without blanks. The 640 ms image duration is ASSUMED. No result is claimed for this software.
notes: Paper (p. 370): the experiment was repeated with the blanks removed; durations are not given. 640 ms per image is ASSUMED so the change rate matches Experiment 1.
Deviation: 12 generated photo-like scene pairs plus procedural pairs replace the paper's 48 photographs; interest was rated by model descriptions (photos) or a placement rule (procedural).
Deviation: a keyed location (4 boxes) and kind report replaces the spoken description; box count, sizes, keys and 20 s report limits are ASSUMED.

tasks.description:
**This set.** Experiment 2. Each image is shown for 560 ms without interruption instead of twice for 240 ms, giving more time to take in each view; the 80 ms blanks between A and A′ stay, so changes still come every 640 ms.

**Question.** A large change in a scene is obvious when it happens in plain view. Is it still easy to see when the moment of change is hidden, and does knowing where to look help?

**What the observer sees.** Grey with an empty white rectangle for [[param:cue_field]], plain grey for [[param:gray_field]], then scene A for [[param:flicker.image]], a grey blank of [[param:flicker.blank]], the changed scene A′ for [[param:flicker.image]], a blank, repeating, for up to [[param:max_flicker]]. The scenes are generated photo-like images and procedural drawings made for this project, not the paper's photographs.

**What they do.** Press [[param:detect_key]] as soon as they see what is changing, then press the numbered box around the change on image A and an arrow key for its kind (appearing, colour or position).

**What varies.** Whether the changed object is of central or marginal interest and the kind of change; here each image stays on longer.

**What is measured.** Alternations until the change is seen (one switch between A and A′ every 640 ms), on trials where the box and the kind were both right: a speed measure.

**What it can and cannot show.** If change blindness came from too little time to take in each image, longer images should make changes much easier to see; the paper reported only a slight speed-up. No result is claimed for this software.
notes: Paper (p. 370): images presented without interruption for 240 + 80 + 240 = 560 ms, blanks between A and A′ kept.
Deviation: 12 generated photo-like scene pairs plus procedural pairs replace the paper's 48 photographs; interest was rated by model descriptions (photos) or a placement rule (procedural).
Deviation: a keyed location (4 boxes) and kind report replaces the spoken description; box count, sizes, keys and 20 s report limits are ASSUMED.

**Question.** A large change in a scene is obvious when it happens in plain view. Is it still easy to see when the moment of change is hidden, and does knowing where to look help?

tasks.description:
**This set.** Experiment 3, partially valid cues. The word names the changing part on half the trials and another part of the scene on the other half, so the observer cannot trust it fully.

**Question.** A large change in a scene is obvious when it happens in plain view. Is it still easy to see when the moment of change is hidden, and does knowing where to look help?

**What the observer sees.** Grey with a white rectangle holding a cue word for [[param:cue_field]], plain grey for [[param:gray_field]], then the Experiment 1 flicker: scene A, grey blank, A, blank, changed scene A′, blank, A′, blank, repeating (images [[param:flicker.image]], blanks [[param:flicker.blank]]), for up to [[param:max_flicker]]. The scenes are generated photo-like images and procedural drawings made for this project, not the paper's photographs.

**What they do.** Press [[param:detect_key]] as soon as they see what is changing, then press the numbered box around the change on image A and an arrow key for its kind (appearing, colour or position).

**What varies.** Whether the changed object is of central or marginal interest and the kind of change, and whether the cue word names the changing part (valid) or another part (invalid), half each.

**What is measured.** Alternations until the change is seen (one switch between A and A′ every 640 ms), on trials where the box and the kind were both right: a speed measure.

**What it can and cannot show.** Faster detection after valid words and slightly slower after invalid ones would show that attention directed by the word, not the word's mere presence, drives the speed-up; the paper reported this. Which trials get a valid word is ASSUMED (alternating within each change type). No result is claimed for this software.
notes: Paper (pp. 370–371): single words or word pairs in the white rectangle for 3 s at the start of each trial. Word choice per scene and rectangle size are ASSUMED (src/rensink1997/photos/spec.json).
Which trials get valid and invalid words is ASSUMED: alternating within each change type in a fixed order.
Deviation: 12 generated photo-like scene pairs plus procedural pairs replace the paper's 48 photographs; interest was rated by model descriptions (photos) or a placement rule (procedural).
Deviation: a keyed location (4 boxes) and kind report replaces the spoken description; box count, sizes, keys and 20 s report limits are ASSUMED.
